skills.title: Nominative: the subject
skills.plain: the nominative (the plain naming form)
skills.summary: The naming form: the subject of the sentence, or a word that renames it after est; singular -a / -us / -um, plural -ae / -i / -a.

skills.title: Grammatical gender
skills.plain: gender (masculine, feminine or neuter, fixed for each noun)
skills.summary: Every noun has a fixed gender: a-nouns are usually feminine, us-nouns masculine, um-nouns neuter; 3rd-declension genders must be learned.

skills.title: Adjective agreement
skills.plain: an adjective agreeing with its noun (same gender, number and case)
skills.summary: An adjective takes the gender, number and case of its noun (malus, mala, malum); the endings need not rhyme with the noun's.

skills.title: Enclitics -que and -ne
skills.plain: the tacked-on words -que ('and') and -ne (turns a sentence into a question)
skills.summary: -que glued to a word means 'and' before it; -ne on the first word marks a yes/no question; -ve means 'or'.

skills.title: Genitive: possession
skills.plain: the genitive (the 'of' form)
skills.summary: The 'whose?' form: -ae / -i singular, -arum / -orum plural; it can stand before or after the noun it belongs to.

skills.title: Genitive: 'of' (description, part, with adjectives)
skills.plain: the genitive (the 'of' form)
skills.summary: The genitive also does the work of English 'of': a cup of wine, a number of sons, full of apples (plenus + genitive).
skills.function: 'of': part, description or after an adjective (a cup of wine, full of apples)

skills.title: Accusative: the object
skills.plain: the accusative (the object form)
skills.summary: The object form: who or what the verb acts on, and the object of most prepositions; -m singular, -s plural; neuters keep the nominative shape.

skills.title: Present tense: he / they (-t, -nt)
skills.plain: the present tense, 3rd person (-t 'he does', -nt 'they do')
skills.summary: A verb is stem + ending: -t for one doer, -nt for several (pulsat, pulsant); the vowel before the ending tells you the conjugation.

skills.title: Imperative: commands
skills.plain: the imperative (the command form)
skills.summary: Orders: the bare stem for one person (tace!, veni!, pone!), stem + -te for several (tacete!); dic, duc, fac drop their final -e.

skills.title: Vocative: calling someone
skills.plain: the vocative (the calling form)
skills.summary: The form for addressing someone: the same as the nominative except -us nouns become -e (Marce!) and -ius nouns become -i (Iuli!, mi fili!).

skills.title: Ablative: place where (in, sub, cum + ablative)
skills.plain: the ablative (the 'in/on/with' form)
skills.summary: Where something is: in, sub, cum, pro take the ablative (-a / -o singular, -is plural); most other prepositions take the accusative.

skills.title: Ablative: from (ab, ex, de + ablative)
skills.plain: the ablative (the 'from' form)
skills.summary: Where something comes from or is separated from: ab, ex, de, sine always take the ablative, whatever their sense (de Deo = about God).
skills.function: from, out of, away from (a / ab / e / ex / de + ablative)

skills.title: Accusative: motion towards (ad, in + accusative)
skills.plain: the accusative (the 'to/into' form after ad, in)
skills.summary: Where something is going: ad, in, sub + accusative (in hortum = into the garden); city names and domum stand alone in the accusative.

skills.title: Ablative: means (by / with a thing)
skills.plain: the ablative (the 'by/with' form)
skills.summary: The thing used to do something goes in the ablative with no preposition (gladio percutit = strikes with a sword); cum is only for company.

skills.title: Passive voice: -tur, -ntur
skills.plain: the passive (the 'is done' form)
skills.summary: The subject has something done to it: -tur (is …-ed) and -ntur (are …-ed) replace -t and -nt; only verbs that take an object can be passive.

skills.title: Ablative of agent: by a person (a/ab + ablative)
skills.plain: the ablative (the 'by' form after a/ab)
skills.summary: With a passive verb the person who does it takes a/ab + ablative (a puero ducitur); a thing used takes the plain ablative of means.
skills.function: agent (by a person: a / ab + ablative)

skills.title: Dative: the indirect object
skills.plain: the dative (the 'to/for' form)
skills.summary: The person something is given, said or shown to: -ae / -o / -i singular, -is / -ibus plural; never marked by word order or a preposition.

skills.title: Demonstratives: hic, ille, is
skills.plain: the pointing words hic ('this'), ille ('that'), is ('that / the one we mean')
skills.summary: hic = this (near), ille = that (far), is = the one already mentioned; they decline like -us -a -um adjectives except genitive -ius and dative -i.

skills.title: Demonstratives standing alone (he, she, it)
skills.plain: a demonstrative used as a pronoun (is = he, ea = she, id = it)
skills.summary: Without a noun, hic / ille / is mean he, she, it, they; the gender follows the noun they stand for (ecce caseus! is malus est).

skills.title: Relative pronoun: qui, quae, quod
skills.plain: the relative pronoun qui, quae, quod ('who, which, that')
skills.summary: qui / quae / quod opens a clause about a noun: gender and number come from that noun, the case from the pronoun's own job in its clause.

skills.title: 3rd declension nouns (masculine and feminine)
skills.plain: a 3rd-declension noun (the -is / -es pattern: pastor, pastoris)
skills.summary: Nouns whose genitive ends in -is: the stem may change (rex, reg-is); endings -em, -is, -i, -e; plural -es, -um / -ium, -ibus.

skills.title: Infinitive: -re and -ri
skills.plain: the infinitive (the 'to' form)
skills.summary: The 'to' form: active -re (ambulare, videre, ponere, audire), passive -ri / -i (videri, poni); used after vult, potest, audet, debet and the like.

skills.title: Accusative + infinitive (indirect statement)
skills.plain: the accusative + infinitive (the 'that …' clause after says / sees / thinks)
skills.summary: After verbs of saying, seeing and thinking the reported subject goes into the accusative and its verb into the infinitive: videt eum aedificare = sees that he is building.

skills.title: 3rd declension neuter nouns
skills.plain: a 3rd-declension neuter noun (corpus, mare: nominative = accusative, plural in -a / -ia)
skills.summary: Neuter 3rd-declension nouns have identical nominative and accusative (caput, corpus), plural -a; nouns in -e / -al / -ar take -ia, -ium and ablative -i (mari).

skills.title: 4th declension nouns (-us, -us)
skills.plain: a 4th-declension noun (the u-pattern: manus, manus)
skills.summary: The u-nouns: -us, -us, -ui, -um, -u; plural -us, -uum, -ibus; mostly masculine (manus is feminine, cornu neuter); domus mixes 4th and 2nd.

skills.title: Dative of possession (mihi est = I have)
skills.plain: the dative of possession (the 'to me there is' way of saying 'I have')
skills.summary: A dative with est says who has something: viro est gladius = the man has a sword; common with names (ei nomen est Marcus) and in relative clauses (cui).

skills.title: Comparative adjectives: -ior, -ius; quam
skills.plain: the comparative (the '-er / more' form)
skills.summary: Add -ior (neuter -ius) to the stem and decline as a 3rd-declension adjective; the thing compared follows quam (fortior quam ille).

skills.title: 5th declension nouns (-es, -ei)
skills.plain: a 5th-declension noun (the e-pattern: dies, diei; res, rei)
skills.summary: The e-nouns: -es, -ei, -ei, -em, -e; plural -es, -erum, -ebus; dies is masculine (feminine for a set date), res feminine.

skills.title: Ablative of time when
skills.plain: the ablative (the 'at / in (a time)' form)
skills.summary: When something happens takes the plain ablative: nocte at night, tertia hora at the third hour, eo tempore at that time; no preposition in Classical Latin.

skills.title: Superlative adjectives: -issimus
skills.plain: the superlative (the '-est / most' form)
skills.summary: -issimus -a -um on the stem (fortissimus); -er adjectives double the r (pulcherrimus); the group compared is genitive or ex + ablative (omnium fortissimus).

skills.title: Present participle: -ns, -ntis
skills.plain: the present participle (the '-ing' word that describes a noun)
skills.summary: Stem + -ns (genitive -ntis): an adjective made from a verb, agreeing with its noun and declined like a 3rd-declension adjective (puer dormiens, pueri dormientis).

skills.title: Personal pronouns: ego, tu, nos, vos, se
skills.plain: the personal pronouns (I, you, we, you all) and the reflexive se ('-self')
skills.summary: ego / tu / nos / vos decline in five cases (me, mihi; te, tibi); se points back to the subject and has no nominative; possession uses meus, tuus, suus, noster, vester.

skills.title: Person endings: -o, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt
skills.plain: the person endings (I / you / he / we / you all / they on the verb)
skills.summary: The ending says who acts: -o I, -s you, -t he/she, -mus we, -tis you all, -nt they; so ego, tu are used only for emphasis.

skills.title: Irregular verbs: sum, possum, eo, volo, nolo, malo, fero
skills.plain: the irregular verbs (be, can, go, want, not want, prefer, carry) in the present
skills.summary: A few common verbs change stem (sum / es, eo / i, vol / vul / vel) or drop the linking vowel (fers, fert, vult); learn them as tables.

skills.title: Deponent verbs: passive form, active meaning
skills.plain: a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks)
skills.summary: Verbs like loquor, sequor, proficiscor have only passive-shaped forms but mean the doing, not the being done; their infinitive ends in -i / -ri.

skills.title: Ablative absolute (noun + participle)
skills.plain: the ablative absolute (a noun + participle set apart in the ablative: 'with X doing')
skills.summary: A noun and a participle both in the ablative give the circumstances of the sentence: sole oriente = as the sun rises; nemine vidente = with nobody watching.

skills.title: Ablative of degree of difference (multo, paulo)
skills.plain: the ablative of degree (the 'by how much' form: multo maior = bigger by much)
skills.summary: How much bigger or smaller: multo fortior = braver by much, decem pedibus altior = ten feet higher; the measure sits in the ablative next to the comparative.

skills.title: Passive person endings: -or, -ris, -tur, -mur, -mini, -ntur
skills.plain: the passive person endings (I am …-ed, you are …-ed …)
skills.summary: -or, -ris, -tur, -mur, -mini, -ntur match -o, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt; the same set serves deponent verbs (sequor, sequeris, sequitur).

skills.title: Adverbs: -e, -iter, and their comparison
skills.plain: an adverb (the '-ly' word: how something is done) and its -ius / -issime forms
skills.summary: -us -a -um adjectives make adverbs in -e (pulchre), 3rd-declension ones in -iter (fortiter); comparative -ius (fortius), superlative -issime (fortissime).

skills.title: Imperfect active: -bam, -bas, -bat
skills.plain: the imperfect (the 'was doing' tense)
skills.summary: Ongoing or repeated past action, and the setting of a story: stem + -ba- + person endings (ambulabat = was walking, used to walk); 3rd conj. adds -e- (ponebat).

skills.title: Imperfect passive and deponent: -batur, -bantur
skills.plain: the imperfect passive (the 'was being done' form)
skills.summary: Same -ba- marker with the passive endings: pulsabatur = was being hit; for deponents the meaning is active (sequebatur = was following).

skills.title: Imperfect of sum, possum, eo: eram, poteram, ibam
skills.plain: the imperfect of the irregular verbs (eram = I was, poteram = I could, ibam = I was going)
skills.summary: sum uses the stem era- (eram, eras, erat …), possum adds pot- (poteram), eo uses i- + -ba- (ibam); volo, fero and the rest are regular (volebat, ferebat).

skills.title: Irregular comparison: bonus, melior, optimus
skills.plain: the irregular comparatives and superlatives (better / best, worse / worst, bigger / biggest)
skills.summary: bonus / melior / optimus, malus / peior / pessimus, magnus / maior / maximus, parvus / minor / minimus, multi / plures / plurimi: new stems, regular endings.

skills.title: Future active: -bo / -am, -es, -et
skills.plain: the future (the 'will do' tense)
skills.summary: 1st and 2nd conjugations add -b- (ambulabo, ambulabis, ambulabit); 3rd and 4th use -a- in the 'I' form and -e- elsewhere (ponam, pones, ponet).

skills.title: Future passive and deponent: -bitur, -etur
skills.plain: the future passive (the 'will be done' form)
skills.summary: The same future markers with passive endings: pulsabitur = will be hit, ponetur = will be put; deponents mean actively (sequetur = will follow).

skills.title: Negative commands: noli / nolite + infinitive
skills.plain: noli / nolite + infinitive (the polite 'don't …')
skills.summary: 'Do not …' is noli (to one person) or nolite (to several) plus the infinitive: noli venire!, nolite timere!; ne + imperative is rare.
skills.highlight_match: nol[iī] \+ infinitive|negative command with nol|prohibition with nol

skills.title: Future of sum, possum, eo: ero, potero, ibo
skills.plain: the future of the irregular verbs (ero = I will be, potero = I will be able, ibo = I will go)
skills.summary: sum uses er- (ero, eris, erit, erunt), possum adds pot- (potero), eo takes -b- (ibo, ibis, ibit); volo and fero go like 3rd-conjugation verbs (volet, feret).

skills.title: Principal parts and the three verb stems
skills.plain: the principal parts (the four dictionary forms that give a verb's present, perfect and participle stems)
skills.summary: ago, agere, egi, actum: the infinitive gives the present stem, the third part the perfect stem (eg-), the fourth the participle stem (act-); 1st, 2nd and 4th conjugations are predictable.

skills.title: Perfect active: -i, -isti, -it, -erunt
skills.plain: the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense)
skills.summary: Completed action or plain past ('did', 'has done'): the perfect stem + -i, -isti, -it, -imus, -istis, -erunt (venit = he came / has come; venerunt = they came).

skills.title: Perfect passive participle: -tus, -sus
skills.plain: the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudatus = praised)
skills.summary: The fourth principal part as an -us -a -um adjective: puer laudatus = the boy (having been) praised; it agrees with its noun like any adjective.

skills.title: Perfect passive: laudatus est
skills.plain: the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudatus est)
skills.summary: Perfect participle + present of sum: visus est = he was seen / has been seen; the participle agrees with the subject (visi sunt), and est translates as 'was'.

skills.title: Perfect infinitive: -isse, -um esse
skills.plain: the perfect infinitive (the 'to have done' form)
skills.summary: Active: perfect stem + -isse (fecisse = to have done); passive: participle + esse (factum esse); used in indirect statement for an earlier action (scit eum venisse).

skills.title: Supine: -um after motion, -u with adjectives
skills.plain: the supine (the special purpose form after a verb of going: dormitum it = goes to sleep)
skills.summary: The participle stem + -um after a verb of motion says why one goes (venatum eo = I go to hunt); the -u form completes an adjective (facile dictu = easy to say).

skills.title: Ablative absolute with a perfect participle
skills.plain: the ablative absolute with a perfect participle ('with X done', 'after X was done')
skills.summary: Noun + perfect participle in the ablative for something already done when the main action happens: hoc dicto = this said; cibo parato = the food prepared.

skills.title: Perfect participle of deponents: 'having done'
skills.plain: the perfect participle of a deponent verb (active meaning: locutus = having spoken)
skills.summary: Deponents form the perfect participle like other verbs but it means 'having done', not 'having been done': puer lapsus = the boy having slipped; femina profecta = the woman having set out.

skills.title: Perfect of deponents: locutus est
skills.plain: the perfect of a deponent verb (locutus est = he spoke)
skills.summary: Participle + sum, translated actively: secutus est = he followed, profecti sunt = they set out; it looks like a perfect passive and never is.
skills.function: perfect of a deponent (locutus est = he spoke)

skills.title: Future participle: -urus, 'about to'
skills.plain: the future participle (the 'about to' word: venturus = about to come)
skills.summary: Participle stem + -ur- + -us -a -um: puer ambulaturus = a boy about to walk, milites morituri = soldiers about to die; futurus = about to be.

skills.title: Future infinitive: -urum esse
skills.plain: the future infinitive (the 'going to' form: venturum esse)
skills.summary: Future participle + esse (often left out) in indirect statement for what will happen: dicit se venturum esse = says that he will come; sum has fore or futurum esse.

skills.title: Pluperfect: -eram, -erat; -us erat
skills.plain: the pluperfect (the 'had done' tense)
skills.summary: Something finished before another past event: perfect stem + -era- + endings (venerat = he had come); passive and deponent use the participle + erat (captus erat, profecti erant).

skills.title: Ablative of comparison (than, without quam)
skills.plain: the ablative of comparison (the 'than' form: illo fortior = braver than he)
skills.summary: Instead of quam + the same case, the thing compared can stand alone in the ablative: hic illo fortior est = this one is braver than that one; nihil hoc peius = nothing worse than this.

skills.title: Deponent imperatives: -re, -mini
skills.plain: the deponent command forms (sequere! = follow!, sequimini! = follow, all of you!)
skills.summary: To one person the deponent imperative looks like an active infinitive (sequere!, intuere!); to several it ends in -mini (sequimini!, laetamini!).

skills.title: Gerund: the verb as a noun (-ndum, -ndi, -ndo)
skills.plain: the gerund (the '-ing' noun form: ad bibendum = for drinking)
skills.summary: Stem + -nd- with neuter endings: ad + -ndum for purpose (ad nandum), -ndi after a noun or with causa (ars scribendi), -ndo for means or after in / de (in ambulando).

skills.title: Present subjunctive: forms (-em, -am; sim, possim, velim)
skills.plain: the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come)
skills.summary: Change the stem vowel: 1st conjugation a → e (ambulet), the others add -a- (videat, ponat, audiat); sum, possum, volo take -i- (sit, possit, velit), eo has eat.

skills.title: Subjunctive on its own: wishes, 'let us', 'let him'
skills.plain: the subjunctive as a wish or gentle command (eamus = let's go; veniat = let him come)
skills.summary: In a main clause the present subjunctive expresses what the speaker wants: a wish (dei te servent), a suggestion (discedamus, let us leave), an order to a third person (veniant); negative ne.
skills.function: wish or command in a main clause (let us …, may he …)

skills.title: Potential subjunctive: 'could', 'would'
skills.plain: the potential subjunctive (the 'could / would / may' form: velim = I would like)
skills.summary: The subjunctive can soften a statement to a possibility: te adiuvem = I could help you; aliquis dicat = someone might say; velim, nolim, malim = I would like / rather not / prefer.

skills.title: Indirect command: ut / ne + subjunctive
skills.plain: ut / ne + subjunctive (the form for what someone asks or orders someone to do)
skills.summary: After verbs of ordering, asking, persuading and wishing (imperat, orat, rogat, monet, vult) the thing wanted goes in ut / ne + subjunctive: imperat ut veniant; orat ne discedat. iubeo instead takes the infinitive.

skills.title: Purpose clause: ut / ne + subjunctive ('in order to')
skills.plain: ut / ne + subjunctive (the 'in order to' clause: venit ut videat = comes to see)
skills.summary: ut + subjunctive says why something is done (veniunt ut cenent = they come in order to dine), ne for a negative aim; a relative qui + subjunctive can do the same job (mittit qui dicat).
skills.highlight_match: purpose clause|relative clause of purpose|clause of purpose

skills.title: Result clause: tam / ita … ut ('so … that')
skills.plain: ut + subjunctive after tam / ita / tantus (the 'so … that' clause)
skills.summary: A signal word (tam so, tantus so big, talis of such a kind, ita in such a way, tot so many) is answered by ut + subjunctive telling what follows; the negative is ut non, never ne.

skills.title: Imperfect subjunctive: forms (infinitive + endings)
skills.plain: the imperfect subjunctive (the past-time 'might / would' form: veniret; built on the infinitive)
skills.summary: The present active infinitive plus person endings: ambulare-t, videre-t, ponere-t, audire-t; passive ponere-tur; irregulars the same way (esse-t, posse-t, velle-t, ferre-t).

skills.title: Sequence of tenses: present vs imperfect subjunctive
skills.plain: the sequence of tenses (a present main verb takes the present subjunctive, a past one the imperfect)
skills.summary: Look at the main verb: present or future → present subjunctive (imperat ut venias); any past tense → imperfect subjunctive (imperavit ut venires). The same holds for purpose, result, cum and indirect questions.

skills.title: cum + subjunctive: 'when / while' in a story
skills.plain: cum + subjunctive (the 'when / while' clause that sets the scene in a past story)
skills.summary: In past narrative cum + imperfect subjunctive = 'while / as' (cum ambularet, latrones vidit), cum + pluperfect = 'after / when he had' (cum dixisset, abiit); cum + ablative is 'with', cum + indicative a plain date.

skills.title: cum + subjunctive: 'since', 'although'
skills.plain: cum + subjunctive meaning 'since' (or, with tamen, 'although')
skills.summary: cum + subjunctive can give the reason (ploro cum mortua sit = I weep since she is dead) or, with tamen in the main clause, a concession (cum dives sit, tamen …); quippe qui + subjunctive = 'as one who'.

skills.title: Indirect question: quis / cur / ubi + subjunctive
skills.plain: an indirect question (a question folded into a sentence: nescio quid faciat = I don't know what he is doing)
skills.summary: After ask, know, tell, wonder, a question word (quis, quid, cur, ubi, quomodo, num, utrum … an) introduces a clause whose verb is subjunctive: sciunt ubi sis; nesciebam quid videret.

skills.title: Deliberative subjunctive: 'what am I to do?'
skills.plain: the deliberative subjunctive (the 'what am I to do?' question: quid faciam?)
skills.summary: A doubtful or despairing question in the subjunctive, usually first person: quid faciam? what am I to do?; quo eamus? where are we to go?; past time uses the imperfect (quid facerem?).
skills.function: deliberative question (what am I to do?)

skills.title: Future perfect: -ero, -erit ('will have done')
skills.plain: the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense)
skills.summary: Perfect stem + -ero, -eris, -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint for an action finished before a future one: cum venero, gaudebo = when I have come, I'll be glad; passive: captus erit.

skills.title: Gerundive: the -ndus adjective
skills.plain: the gerundive (the '-nd-' adjective: 'to be done'; aqua bibenda = water to be drunk)
skills.summary: Stem + -nd- + -us -a -um, agreeing with a noun: what should be done to it (liber legendus); after ad or with causa it replaces gerund + object (ad litteras scribendas = for writing letters).

skills.title: Gerundive + sum: 'must be done'
skills.plain: the gerundive with sum (the 'must be done' pattern: liber legendus est = the book must be read)
skills.summary: Gerundive + a form of sum says what needs doing: cibus comedendus est = the food must be eaten; with no subject it is impersonal (dormiendum est = one must sleep); in indirect statement -ndum esse.

skills.title: Dative of agent with the gerundive (mihi = by me)
skills.plain: the dative of agent (the person who must do it: mihi legendum est = I must read)
skills.summary: With the gerundive + sum the doer goes in the dative, not a/ab + ablative: liber mihi legendus est = the book must be read by me, I have to read the book; servis laborandum est.
skills.function: agent with the gerundive (by whom it must be done)

skills.title: Perfect subjunctive: -erim, -eris, -erit
skills.plain: the perfect subjunctive (the 'have done' form: nescio quid fecerit; ne timueris = don't be afraid)
skills.summary: Perfect stem + -eri- + endings (fecerim, feceris, fecerit …; passive factus sim) for a completed action after a present main verb: nescio quis venerit; cum clauserit; and ne + 2nd person for 'don't' (ne timueris). -eris / -erit / -erint also spell the future perfect.

skills.title: Wishes: utinam + subjunctive
skills.plain: utinam + subjunctive (the 'if only …' wish; the tense says whether it can still come true)
skills.summary: utinam (negative utinam ne) + present subjunctive = a wish that may still happen (utinam veniat); + imperfect = a present wish that cannot (utinam venirent, if only they were coming); + pluperfect = a past one (utinam venisset).

skills.title: Pluperfect subjunctive: -issem, -isset
skills.plain: the pluperfect subjunctive (the 'had / would have' form: cum venisset = when he had come)
skills.summary: The perfect infinitive + endings (fecisse-m, fecisse-t; passive factus essem) for an action completed before a past main verb: cum advenissent, cibum sumpserunt; nesciebam quis advenisset.

skills.title: Unreal conditions: si + imperfect / pluperfect subjunctive
skills.plain: the contrary-to-fact condition (si + subjunctive: 'if I were …, I would …'; 'if I had …, I would have …')
skills.summary: Imperfect subjunctive in both halves for an unreal present (si thunnus essem, in mari habitarem = if I were a tuna I would live in the sea); pluperfect for an unreal past (si bibisset, non mortuus esset); tamquam takes the same tenses.
skills.function: unreal condition (if I were …, if I had …)

skills.title: Future imperative: esto, memento, -to
skills.plain: the future imperative (the 'you shall …' order for later or for rules: esto! memento!)
skills.summary: Stem + -to (plural -tote, 3rd person -nto) gives an order for the future or a standing rule: esto = be (from now on), memento = remember, scito = know that; common in laws and maxims.

skills.title: Verbs that take the dative (pareo, placeo, noceo, credo)
skills.plain: the dative (the 'to/for' form)
skills.summary: Some verbs put their object in the dative where English has a direct object: pareo obey, placeo please, noceo harm, credo believe, persuadeo persuade, ignosco forgive, and compounds of sum (adsum, prosum): servi domino parent.
skills.function: object of a dative verb (pareo, placeo, noceo, credo …)
skills.highlight_match: verb taking the dative|impersonal verb with the dative|verb with the dative

skills.title: dummodo + subjunctive: 'provided that'
skills.plain: dummodo + subjunctive (the 'provided that / as long as' condition)
skills.summary: dummodo (also modo, dum) + subjunctive states a condition that must hold: oderint dum metuant = let them hate, provided they fear; negative dummodo ne.

skills.title: Metre: hexameter, pentameter and hendecasyllable
skills.plain: the metre (the rhythm of a line: the hexameter and pentameter of the elegiac couplet, Catullus's eleven-syllable line)
skills.summary: The dactylic hexameter (six feet, long-short-short or long-long) alternates with the pentameter (two halves of two and a half feet) in the elegiac couplet of Ovid and Martial; Catullus's hendecasyllable has eleven syllables.

skills.title: Prosody: long and short syllables, elision
skills.plain: prosody (which syllables count long or short, and when a final vowel is swallowed by the next word)
skills.summary: A syllable is long if its vowel is long, a diphthong, or followed by two consonants; a final vowel or -m before a word starting with a vowel or h- is elided (od(i) et amo); the hexameter pauses at a caesura.
